title: Slavery and the slave trade, 1850
snippet: Free and slave states and territories in late 1850, the Missouri Compromise line, the routes of the slave trade within the United States, and the approximate routes of the Underground Railroad.
description:
Question: Where was slavery legal in 1850, and how were enslaved people moved, or how did they escape?

What the map shows: The states and territories of late 1850, after California became a state, are shaded in four groups: free states, slave states (and Washington, D.C.), free territories and territories open to slavery. A dashed line marks the Missouri Compromise line. Click an area for its group and a one-sentence reason. Four more layers are off when the map opens: the routes of the slave trade within the United States, the routes of the ships La Amistad (1839) and Creole (1841), and the approximate routes and cities of the Underground Railroad. Turn them on in the layer list.

Notes: Outlines and routes come from a map of 1850 in Harper's Atlas of American History (1920), digitized by Esri, so they are approximate, and boundaries in the West are drawn as on that map. The atlas classes each area by the law that made it free or slave; this map uses four plain groups instead. A free state was not always free for everyone: the pop-up for New Jersey explains one case. The Underground Railroad was secret, so its routes are approximate. Route lines do not show direction; the pop-up gives it.

Sources: Dixon Ryan Fox, Harper's Atlas of American History (1920), plate "Slavery and Slave Trade, 1830-1850", digitized by Esri; acts of Congress and state admission records, fact-checked 11 November 2026; Esri basemap.
